Screenshot S2 - prompt-injection input (same type as Test 13; the injection answer from the iteration experiment): v1 treats it as a normal answer, v4 flags the injection, ignores it and scores only the real content (2/5).
Screenshot S3 - Tests 1 and 8 in the live interview flow: P1 question for Software Engineer Intern (Technical), P2 scores with verified quotes, and the P3 follow-up on the weakest area (depth).
iter_reading: v1 was already steady on this model (3 in all 5 runs), so its problems were format and fairness, not randomness: 0/11 parseable JSON, one number with no per-criterion breakdown or evidence, 5/5 for both wordings of the full answer, and 'idk' and the injection answer just got 1 with no flag. v2 fixed the format (11/11 JSON) but casual wording scored 0.62 lower than the same content written formally. v3 removed run-to-run variation (range 0) and added quoted evidence, but 2 of 28 quotes were not in the answer and the style gap grew to 0.75. v4 cut the style gap to 0.25, marked 'idk' invalid (score 0), flagged the injection (score 2.0), and all 21 quotes were verbatim. The style gap is smaller but not zero, so it is listed as a limitation.
test_reading: 22 of 23 tests passed. The failed test, T23, is the cross-model check: on Gemma 4 31B one of six evidence quotes was not in the student's answer. The code check removed it before the student saw it, which is why that check exists. Close calls: T10 passed exactly at the 0.5 limit, and T6 and T18 got a perfect 5.0, which may mean the evaluator is generous with strong answers. An earlier run on the same day failed T1-T4 because of a threading bug in our code (a shared API client was closed while in use); we fixed it in llm.py and re-ran the whole suite.
